General safety information
Important safety instructions
1.1 Important safety instructions
It is important to install, operate, maintain, and dispose of the equipment according to the
information in the product documentation, and in compliance with local regulations. For the
safety of the users and the patients, before a user operates or works on the equipment, they
must read, understand, and obey all:
• Warnings, cautions, instructions, and notes in this document and the related
documents.
• Safety instructions, emergency procedures, and information in this document and the
related documents.
• Warnings, cautions, and safety markings on the equipment and the accessories of the
equipment.
If you have local work instructions for the equipment, then Elekta recommends that you include
the warnings, cautions, and notes from this document in your local work instructions.
1.1.1 Conventions for warnings, cautions, and notes
The conventions give information about the class and the level of the risk in the warnings and
cautions, and the content of notes.
WARNING 1.1
A warning is information about procedures, tasks, or conditions with a risk of fatal or serious
injury, injury, or clinical mistreatment, if you do not obey the instructions.
CAUTION 1.1
A caution is information about procedures, tasks, or conditions with a risk of damage to the
equipment, data, or the environment, if you do not obey the instructions.
Note: A note gives more information about a related text.
1.1.2 Expected service life of the equipment
The expected service life is the length of time that the regular service and repair procedures can
keep the equipment safe to operate.
WARNING 1.2
Do not operate the equipment unless you correctly complete the safety checks, planned
maintenance schedules, and extended life checks. If you ignore this warning, you can cause
fatal injury and damage to the equipment.
The expected service life of this equipment is 15 years of normal use.
The Elekta definition for 'expected service life' is the length of time that the regular service and
repair procedures can keep the equipment safe to operate.
The Elekta definition of 'normal use' is the treatment of 50 patients each day for five days each
week of the year. If the equipment is used more frequently than this, the frequency of the
planned maintenance must increase accordingly and the extended life checks must also be
brought forward accordingly.

General safety information
Important safety instructions
The level of operation of the equipment can be different to ‘normal use’. This has an effect on the
length of the service life. Because of wear of parts, the risk of a malfunction can increase after 10
years operation. Elekta recommends that before you continue operation after 10 years, you
complete the regular extended life checks.
Elekta can help the User with the correct safety checks, planned maintenance schedules, and the
regular extended life checks for continued safe operation of the equipment.
The system must be maintained throughout its expected service life in compliance with the EMC
information detailed in the applicable Instructions for Use.
For information on the above checks and schedules, contact your local Elekta representative.

1.2 Safety precautions
1.2.1 Safety precautions for the compatibility of the equipment
WARNING 1.3
Do not use parts, accessories, or other equipment, without approval by Elekta of their
compatibility. If you ignore this warning, you can cause fatal injury and damage to the
equipment.
Only operate the equipment with Elekta supplied or approved, compatible equipment or parts.
Accessories, transducers, and cables that are not specified by or do not have the approval of
Elekta can cause an incorrect treatment delivery. They can also have an effect on the performance
of the electromagnetic compatibility (EMC), which can increase the emissions or decrease the
immunity of the equipment.
Contact Elekta for information about the compatibility of other equipment or parts.
1.2.2 Safety precautions for the electromagnetic compatibility
The design and manufacture of Elekta products is in compliance with applicable EMC standards.
The intended result of the standards is to minimize the risk of electromagnetic interference by RF
devices. The type of device and the distance to the equipment has an effect on the intensity of
the electromagnetic interference. The equipment includes the linear accelerator and accessories,
the control cabinets, the computers in the control room, and equipment from other
manufacturer.

General safety information
Safety precautions
It is necessary to have special precautions for EMC emissions. Elekta recommends that you obey
these precautions when you use RF devices near the equipment.
• Do not use RF devices unless they are in compliance with international standards for
electromagnetic compatibility, for example, the CE or FCC mark.
• Do not use a two-way emergency radio in the treatment room or the control room.
Only use an emergency radio if there is an emergency.
• Do not use cellular telephones, or other devices with cellular modems near the
equipment. The Instructions for Use contains information on the minimum safe
distance of these devices from the equipment.
• When you use a device that is enabled for wireless operation, it must be a minimum of
10 cm from the equipment.
• Radio-Frequency Identification (RFID) readers, when activated to do a scan of a RFID
tag, must be a minimum of one meter from the equipment.
Note: The RFID systems that Elekta supply use lower power levels. You can safely use these RFID systems
when you obey the procedures in the Instructions for Use for the product.
The system must be installed, put into service, and maintained in compliance with the EMC
information in the Instructions for Use.
Contact Elekta for information about the compatibility of parts and equipment.
WARNING 1.4
Do not put portable or mobile radio frequency (RF) communication devices near to the
equipment. The emissions from such RF devices can be more than the EMC standards, and can
have unwanted effects on the equipment operation. If you ignore this warning, the RF
emissions can cause the equipment to have a malfunction. A malfunction can cause fatal injury,
clinical mistreatment, or damage to the equipment.
WARNING 1.5
Do not use accessories, transducers, and cables that are not specified by Elekta. They can have
an effect on the EMC performance, which can increase EMC emissions or decrease the
immunity to RF interference of the equipment. If you ignore this warning, incorrect radiation
delivery and other malfunctions can occur, which can cause fatal injury or clinical mistreatment.
1.2.3 Safety precaution for Service Tools and lifting equipment
WARNING 1.6
Do not use defective or damaged lifting equipment. If you ignore this warning, you can cause
fatal injury and damage to the equipment.
WARNING 1.7
Do not use incorrectly calibrated or defective Service Tools. If you ignore this warning, you can
cause injury and damage to the equipment.
Before you use the Service Tool or lifting equipment, make sure that:
• There are no defective or damaged parts
• The calibration of the Service Tool is correct

1.2.4 Safety precaution for work with electrical and mechanical parts
WARNING 1.8
Do not connect any electrical power supply before the ground earth connections are secure.
There is a risk of high leakage current. If you ignore this warning, you can cause fatal injury.
WARNING 1.9
Do not remove the cables or the covers, or operate the equipment without the covers. If you
ignore this warning, you can cause fatal injury
The covers on the equipment prevent access to high voltage parts and parts that move. If you
remove the covers, there is a risk of high voltage shock or injury from parts that move.
Only remove the covers if you are an Elekta approved person with the correct authority and you
obey the applicable safety procedures.
1.2.5 Safety precaution for work with safety devices during service
operation
WARNING 1.10
Do not remove, change, or override the safety switches, interlocks, and other safety devices. If
you ignore this warning, you can cause fatal injury or clinical mistreatment.
The procedures in this document can tell you to remove, change, or override the safety switches,
interlocks, or other safety devices during repair or maintenance work. When the work is
completed, make all the safety devices active again, and do a test of them.
1.2.6 Safety precaution for work on BLDs with UV lighting
WARNING 1.11
Do not look into the ultraviolet lighting of the BLD without protective glasses. If you ignore this
warning, you can cause serious injury.
The covers and screens of the BLD prevent an injury to your eyes from the ultraviolet lighting.
Before you remove the covers or screens of the BLD, switch off the linear accelerator, or use
protective glasses. Protective glasses must have the UV-A specification OD 6+ @ 190 - 532 Nm.
If there is damage to the covers or screen of the BLD, switch off the linear accelerator and contact
the Elekta representative.

Safety precautions
1.2.7 Safety precaution for work with lasers
WARNING 1.12
Do not look into the laser beams because they can cause damage to your eyes. If you ignore
this warning, you can cause serious injury.
Elekta systems use the laser beams to help set up patients in the correct position for treatment.
During your work in the treatment room, make sure that you do not look into the laser beams.
1.2.8 Safety precautions for work with display screen equipment
WARNING 1.13
Do not use the display screen equipment for long periods of time. If you ignore this warning,
you can cause injury.
When you use the display screen equipment (DSE), obey the applicable Health and Safety
regulations and procedures in the jurisdiction where you do the work.
1.2.9 Safety precautions for cleaning and disinfection
WARNING 1.14
Do not clean the equipment, or use a disinfectant spray when the equipment is connected to
the electrical supply. If you ignore this warning, you can cause fatal injury.
WARNING 1.15
Do not use a spray that is explosive or flammable. If you ignore this warning, you can cause
fatal injury and damage to the equipment.
CAUTION 1.2
Do not let water and other liquids go into the equipment. If you ignore this caution, you can
cause damage to the equipment.
CAUTION 1.3
Do not use a spray to clean the medical equipment room. If you ignore this caution, you can
cause damage to the equipment.
At regular intervals, it is necessary to clean the equipment and equipment room with
disinfectants. Elekta recommends that the procedures to clean the equipment and the equipment
room obey the applicable laws and regulations of the jurisdiction where the equipment is
installed.

General safety information
Safety precautions
1.2.10 Safety precautions for work with high temperatures on the BLD
covers
During normal operation, the maximum temperatures of the accessory ring and BLD outer covers
can increase to 45 °C. Make sure that you do not touch the outer covers or the accessory ring for
more than 1 minute.
1.2.11 Safety precaution for the installation of accessories on the BLD
WARNING 1.16
Do not touch the connector found in the accessory ring on the BLD. If you ignore this warning,
you can cause injury.
When you install an accessory, for example, a shadow tray, electron applicator, or front pointer,
do not touch the pins in the connector. The pins have a low electrical current, which can give an
electric shock when you touch them.
1.2.12 Safety precautions for work with heavy parts
The safety precautions for work with heavy parts are the necessary safety precautions to know to
prevent injury.
WARNING 1.17
Do not lift or move heavy parts unless you obey the applicable Health and Safety regulations
and procedures. If you ignore this warning, you can cause serious injury.
1.2.13 Safety precautions during work on the BLD
When you do work on the BLD, make sure that you obey the following safety precautions:
WARNING 1.18
Do not do work on the inner parts of the beam limiting device while the electrical supply is
connected. There is a risk of high voltage electric shock. If you ignore this warning, you can
cause fatal injury.
WARNING 1.19
Do not do work on the beam limiting device unless the gantry is at 0° or 180°. Gravity can cause
the leaves, diaphragms, and dynamic leaf guides to move. If you ignore this warning, you can
cause fatal injury.
WARNING 1.20
Do not touch the hot LED field light projector, or the heat sink, immediately after operation. If
you ignore this warning, you can cause serious injury.

General safety information
Safety precautions
1.2.14 Safety precaution for the removal of parts from the radiation head
WARNING 1.21
Do not touch the flight tube, bending magnet, or other parts near to them until a check for
induced radioactivity is completed. Excessive exposure to radioactivity is dangerous. If you
ignore this warning, you can cause serious injury.
After the operation of the linear accelerator at high energy, the parts in the radiation head can
become radioactive and a radiation hazard. Before you do work on, or remove parts from the
radiation head, use a calibrated radiation detector to measure the level of induced radioactivity.
Use the applicable safety procedures when you remove radioactive parts and material. The
maximum dose rate for the safe removal of radioactive parts and material is 50 µSv/hr
(microsievert per hour). Do not remove the radioactive parts and material from the treatment
room before they are correctly prepared for safe removal.
1.2.15 Safety precautions for maintenance, modification, and
decommissioning
WARNING 1.22
Do not do work, or make modifications to the equipment without the correct training and
authority. If you ignore this warning, you can cause fatal injury, clinical mistreatment, and
damage to the equipment.
Only do work on, or make modifications to, the equipment if you are an Elekta approved person
with the applicable authority. Such work must use best practice and obey the laws and
regulations in the jurisdiction in which the equipment is installed.
Modifications or work that does not have approval by Elekta, and is not done by an Elekta
approved person with the correct authority, can cause:
• Fatal injury
• Incorrect radiation delivery
• Malfunction of the equipment
• Damage to the equipment
• The warranty to be canceled.
1.2.16 Safety precautions for work in areas of induced radioactivity
The safety precautions for work in areas of induced radioactivity are the precautions to prevent
an excessive exposure to, and serious injury from, induced radioactivity.
When you operate or do work on the equipment, Elekta recommends that you use the applicable
radiation protection functions, devices, systems, procedures, and accessories. Always obey the
applicable laws and regulations for induced radioactivity for the jurisdiction in which the
equipment is installed.
The safety precautions are applicable to:
• Maintenance, modifications, and decommissioning
• Measurement of the induced radioactivity
• Removal and movement of parts with induced radioactivity.

General safety information
Safety precautions
1.2.16.1 Safety precautions for the measurement of induced radioactivity
The safety precautions for the measurement of induced radioactivity are the necessary safety
precautions to know to prevent excessive exposure to radioactivity, which can cause serious
injury or damage to the environment.
Always use two radiation detectors to measure the level of induced radioactivity. Only use
radiation detectors that have an applicable calibration certificate. The period of time since the
last calibration date must be less than 12 months. Do not use the radiation detectors if the period
of time since the last calibration date is more than 12 months.
WARNING 1.23
Do not move radioactive material (by air, sea, or land) unless you obey the applicable laws and
regulations for induced radioactivity and disposal of radioactive material of the jurisdictions
through which the movement occurs. If you ignore this warning, you can cause serious injury
and damage to the environment.
1.2.16.2 Safety precautions for handling parts with induced radioactivity
The handling of parts with induced radioactivity must comply with the laws and regulations of the
jurisdiction in which the equipment is installed. The safe levels of radiation applicable in the UK
do not apply in all jurisdictions. The permitted level of radioactivity must always be as low as
reasonably achievable (ALARA). This level may vary depending on local rules, therefore the safe
working levels from the applicable local rules must be considered as the acceptable working limit.
If there are no safe levels available for a jurisdiction, use the UK value as a guideline, which is a
maximum of 150 cps at the surface for a maximum duration of 72 minutes. The following table
shows the conversion from this value to other units.

1.3 Emergencies
1.3.1 Safety precaution for the occurrence of fire or explosion
WARNING 1.24
Do not use the equipment in rooms that contain explosive or flammable gases. If you ignore
this warning, you can cause fatal injury and damage to the equipment.

Before you use the equipment, Elekta recommends that you know all the local emergency
procedures and the locations of all the emergency switches.
The Elekta equipment includes:
• The STOP MOTORS buttons on the handheld controllers and user interface panels in
the treatment room, and FKP in the control room.
When you press these buttons, it disconnects the electrical supply from the motors,
stops all movements of the equipment, and stops kV and MV radiation.
• The EMERGENCY POWER OFF buttons in the treatment room, control area, and areas
near the equipment.
When you operate these buttons, it disconnects the electrical supply to the linear
accelerator. The buttons disconnect the electrical supply from many electrical circuits,
but not from all the circuits.

2.1.3 Disposal of the equipment
End of life (EOL) disposal is the procedure to disassemble, remove, and discard the equipment, in
full or in parts, to a condition where it is not possible to operate the equipment for its intended
use.
Only a Qualified Expert (QE) and an approved facility with an applicable license, may remove and
discard the equipment and recycle the material.
A full description of disposal requirements is detailed in a separate document Product Disposal
Information. This document is available on request from Elekta.
The customer owns the data on the storage media. If there are any data storage media such as
HDDs, remove them from the device and hand them to the customer for disposal. If the customer
entrusts the disposal team to dispose of the data, the data must be destroyed in accordance with
relevant cybersecurity regulations.

Do not touch the parts identified with the ESD caution label. Always obey the ESD precautions

electrostatic discharge. To prevent the ESD damage to these devices, always wear a grounded
antistatic wrist strap, and obey the applicable ESD precautions and procedures.

ESD caution label and these ESD precautions.

Introduction
Document scope
3.1 Document scope
The corrective maintenance manual (CMM) helps service engineers troubleshoot, repair and
maintain the systems, subsystems and components of the linear accelerator. The target audience
is qualified service engineers. These may be engineers employed directly by Elekta, qualified
representatives of Elekta or qualified representatives of Elekta's customers.
The manual provides:
• A description of the system or sub-system in question.
• A troubleshooting section to identify the problem areas.
• A set of detailed procedures used to replace FRUs (field replaceable units).
• A section on how to return the device to work.
If you find any mistakes in this document, or identify areas for improvement, please raise a CLM
(customer lifecycle management) case and assign it to the relevant queue.

Product description
System overview
4.1 System overview
The iViewGT™ imaging system is an MV electronic portal imaging detector (EPID) that uses the Xray radiation of the linear accelerator and an MV detector panel to capture an image of the
patient. The image shows the position of the patient in relation to the radiation beam.
The imaging system has four subsystems:
• The imaging arm with the MV detector panel
The MV detector panel in the imaging arm contains a Scintillator that changes the
incident X-ray radiation to light. An array of amorphous silicon (a-Si) photodiodes
below the Scintillator captures the light and changes it to voltage levels that are
related to the amount of incident X-ray radiation. The internal electronics of the
detector panel changes the output voltages of the photodiodes to digital values that
are put together row by row to make the image data. The image data is then
transferred from the MV detector panel to the control cabinet on a dedicated data
connection. The DCB sends signals to the MV detector panel to make sure that the
acquired images are synchronized with the linear accelerator.
• The mechanical arm movements system
An HHC sends signals to the ACB, which controls the power to the motors in the
imaging arm. The motors move the imaging arm in the G-T direction and the MV
detector panel in the G-T direction and A-B direction.
• The imaging control cabinet
The imaging control cabinet contains the imaging system software, a CAN bus PCB, a
frame grabber PCB (AL detector panel only) and an Ethernet connection to the local
network. There is a dedicated LAN connection for imaging systems with an AP detector
panel.
Note: The frame grabber PCB (AL detector panel only) is not applicable for Harmony.
• The power supply chassis (Area 44)
The detector PSU and the detector arm movement PSUs are in the power supply
chassis in Area 44 behind the gantry drum. Area 44 also contains the power supplies
for the XVI system.

The detector panel transfers image data to the imaging control cabinet between the radiation
pulses of the digital accelerator. Synchronization pulses sent from the digital accelerator PPG are
changed to optical signals and sent to the DCB. The DCB uses these pulses to cause the detector
panel to read the image data from the sensor array. The imaging control cabinet receives the
image data on a dedicated data connection from the MV detector panel.
For the AL detector panel, a frame grabber PCB in the imaging control cabinet receives the image
data from the detector panel. For the AP detector panel, the imaging control cabinet receives the
image data on a Gigabit Ethernet connection.
Note: The AL detector panel is not applicable for Harmony.
After a complete frame is transferred, the DCB sends a frame synchronization signal on the CAN
bus to the imaging control cabinet. This causes the imaging system software to apply corrections
to the image data.
The imaging system software corrects the image for offset, gain calibration and bad pixels. The
offset applies a correction for the imaging system dark current. The system uses an automated
offset image capture to make sure that the correction procedure uses the latest imaging system
dark current values. The gain calibration applies a correction for the sensitivity of different pixels.
The bad pixel correction applies a software correction for unserviceable pixels.
The imaging system continuously monitors for problems. If a problem occurs, a message is
displayed in the imaging system software before the image capture starts. Log files are used to
record the error information for the imaging and iCom systems.

4.2.1 Operation of the trigger system of the AL detector panel (nonapplicable for Harmony)
The trigging system of the AL detector panel makes sure that transfer of image data can only
occur between radiation pulses. The DCB uses the gun pulse from the PPG of the digital
accelerator to control the acquisition and transfer of image data to the imaging control cabinet.
The detector panel receives trigger signals from the DCB. The trigger signals cause the detector
panel to read two rows of sensor data, one row from each end of the detector panel sensor array.
The detector panel combines the row data to form a single data packet, which it sends to the
frame grabber PCB in the iViewGT™ control cabinet. As more trigger signals occur, the detector
panel reads two more rows. This continues from the outer edges to the center of the detector
panel sensor array.
After the detector panel reads a complete frame, a frame synchronization signal is sent from the
detector panel to the DCB. The DCB then sends a packet of data to the iViewGT™ control cabinet
on the CAN bus. The packet of data includes the PRF and other information. The iViewGT™
system software attaches the packet of data to the frame. The acquired image data is put into a
buffer for the iViewGT™ system software to apply corrections.

The DCB sends trigger signals to the detector panel between the gun pulses. When the gun pulse
PRF is 400 pulses per second (not de-tuned for an FTM system), the time period between pulses
is 2.5 ms. In this time period, the DCB sends four trigger signals to the detector panel. The
detector panel reads two lines of image data for each trigger signal it receives and therefore it
acquires eight lines of image data. To read a complete frame of 1024 lines, 128 gun pulses are
necessary and the total time to read the frame is approximately 320 ms.
If the PRF changes to 200 pulses per second, the time period between pulses is 5 ms. The DCB
sends eight trigger signals to the detector panel. As before, the detector panel reads two lines of
image data for each trigger signal. To read a complete frame of 1024 lines, 64 gun pulses are
necessary and the total time to read the frame continues to be approximately 320 ms.
Regardless of the PRF, the DCB provides sufficient trigger signals between the gun pulses to read a
frame in 320 ms.
PSP detector panels
For detector panels with a PSP upgrade, the time to read a complete frame of data is longer. If the
gun pulse PRF is 400 pulses per second, the time period between pulses is 2.5 ms, but the DCB
only sends three trigger signals to the detector panel. The detector panel reads two lines of image
data for each trigger signal it receives and therefore it acquires six lines of image data. To read a
complete frame of 1024 lines, approximately 170 gun pulses are necessary and the total time to
read the frame is 427 ms.

For FTM and non-FTM digital accelerators, the DCB sends start and stop trigger signals to the
detector panel between the gun pulses (see Figure 4.10). For example, when the gun pulse PRF is
400 pulses per second (not de-tuned for an FTM system), the time period between pulses is

image data from the sensor array. When the detector panel reads a row, it sends the image data
over a dedicated Gigabit Ethernet connection to the imaging control cabinet and sends a trigger
signal to the DCB. The DCB counts the number of trigger signals it receives and when the DCB
receives 20 trigger signals, it sends a stop signal to the detector panel. This sequence continues
until all the image data is read from the sensor array. To read a complete frame of 1024 lines,
approximately 51 gun pulses are necessary and the total time to read the frame is approximately

4.2.3 Description of the frame pre-averaging procedure
The AP MV detector panel can supply frames to the imaging software at approximately eight
frames per second. To maintain the throughput of frames, the imaging system software averages
three frames before it puts the result in a first in first out buffer.
Pre-averaged frames are taken from the buffer and corrected for gain and offset. The imaging
system software monitors the size of the buffer. If it grows larger than five frames, the message
that follows appears in the sri.log file.
• GainOffsetCorrector::ProcessImageQueue Buffer Size = 5.
When the imaging system software receives a frame, it sends a message to tell the detector panel
that a frame was received. If the imaging system software receives a frame, but does not send a
message to the detector panel, the message that follows appears in the sri.log file.
• Detector Panel dropped at least one frame.

4.3.1 Description of the offset image corrections
To apply an offset image correction, it is necessary for the imaging system to make and save offset
images. The imaging system continuously reads frames from the detector panel. Some of these
frames are used to make offset images.
The imaging system makes and saves a new offset image if:
• There is a change in energy that causes a change in the exposure gain setting (AP panel
only).
• The radiation is off for more than the specified number of image frames
(AutoOffsetMinBeamOffFrames).
• The imaging system captures the correct quantity of image frames for an offset image
(AutoOffsetMinFrames).
The AL and AP detector panels have the same values for the offset parameters in the sri.ini
file (see Table 4.2).
Note: The AL detector panel is not applicable for Harmony.

Because of the different frequencies used on an FTM digital accelerator, different offset

4.3.2 Description of the first and second stage radiation synchronization
calibration
The calibration sequence is:
• Offset
• First stage radiation synchronization
• Gain
• Second stage radiation synchronization.
The first stage calibration procedure uses a PRF of 5 to acquire an image. The procedure applies
an offset correction to the image before it identifies the pixels with pulse line artifacts. It uses
these pixels and the pixels in the area that does not have pulse line artifacts to calculate the
correction factors. The first stage calibration procedures save the correction factors in the
sri.ini file.
The gain calibration procedure uses the first stage correction factors to give images without pulse
line artifacts.
The second stage calibration acquires an image at a PRF of 5 with a wedge field and the collimator
set at 90°. This gives a vertical intensity gradient that is perpendicular to the pulse line artifacts.
The effect is to emulate different dose rates and intensity changes in clinical images. Before the
procedure calculates the correction factors, it applies the offset and gain calibration corrections.
To calculate the correction factors, it uses almost the same procedure as the first stage
calibration. The second stage calibration procedure saves the correction factors in the sri.ini
file where it overwrites the first stage correction factors.
For the AP panel there are 20 correction factors for each low, middle, and high energy.
For the AL panel (non-applicable for Harmony) there are eight correction factors, four for the top
section and four for the lower section. There is also a set of eight correction factors for each low,
middle, and high energy.
4.3.3 Description of the single level gain calibration
A single level gain calibration is necessary at each energy to correct for the differences in gain
response of the pixels in the sensor array of the MV detector panel. The gain calibration also
calibrates the image dose.
The Energies parameter in the sri.ini file sets the number of energies for calibration.
When set correctly, the system automatically moves the user through the gain calibration
procedure in the correct sequence.
The gain calibration procedure is available in the Service menu.

4.3.4 Description of the multilevel gain calibration
Multilevel gain calibration corrects for different levels of dose on the detector because of
attenuation by the patient. The correction is more accurate because it is related to the pixel
output value. In contrast, a single level gain uses one dose level to correct the images and
assumes a linear relationship of dose to pixel output value, where the relationship is not actually
linear.
A multilevel gain calibration takes longer to do than a single level gain calibration. For example, a
five-level multilevel gain calibration takes three times longer than a single level calibration. Only
do a multilevel gain calibration if it is necessary.

4.3.5 Description of the Beam Modulator™ calibration (AL panel (nonapplicable for Harmony))
For a Beam Modulator™ single level gain calibration, the imaging system captures images at five
positions. The imaging system then puts the images together to make one gain calibration image
for each energy. For a multilevel gain calibration, the imaging system captures a single image for
each gain level.
An example of the syntax of the filename for the Beam Modulator™ multilevel gain calibration is:
BM_H_000_1_0.his
The syntax of the file name is:
• BM is the image description
• H is the X-ray energy (L = Low, H = High or M = Mid)
• 000 is a constant (always 000)
• 1 the detector panel position (range 1 to 5)
• 0 is the gain level (range 0 to 7).
Therefore, the example file name BM_H_000_1_0.his holds a Beam Modulator™ image at
high energy for gain level 0.
The imaging system combines the images to make flood and gain images at the X-ray energy and
each gain level (if it is necessary).
For single level gain, an example of the syntax of the file names for the images put together is:
FLDH000.his and GAINH000.his
The syntax of the file name is:
• FLD is the Flood image
• GAIN is the Gain image
• 000 is a constant (always 000)
• H is the X-ray energy (L = Low, H = High or M = Mid).
Therefore, the example files FLDH000.his and GAINH000.his are for flood and gain images
at high energy.
For multilevel gain, an example of the syntax of the filename for the images put together is:
FLOOD_H_000_1.his
The syntax of the file name is:
• FLOOD is the image description, in this example it is a “flood” image
• H is the X-ray energy (L = Low, H = High or M = Mid)
• 000 is a constant that is always 000
• 1 the detector panel position 1 to 5
• 0 is the number of gain level with a range of 0 to 7.
Therefore, the example file FLOOD_H_000_1.his holds a flood image at high energy for gain
level 1.

4.3.6 Description of the bad pixel map
A bad pixel map identifies pixels that the imaging system cannot correct with gain or offset
correction. The value of each unserviceable pixel is set to the average value of its adjacent pixels.
The manufacturer supplies a bad pixel map on a CD with a new detector panel. A copy of this
image is installed in the imaging system software folder during the installation procedure. If the
bad pixel map changes during the life of the detector panel, use the X-ray imaging software (XIS)
to make a new one.

4.3.7 Description of the noise reduction filter
You can configure the two settings that follow to adjust the noise reduction filter that iViewGT™
applies to the MV images:
• A salt and pepper noise removal filter
• A smoothing despeckle filter.
The salt and pepper despeckle filter replaces the center pixel with the median value of the kernel
if it has the highest or lowest value compared to the adjacent pixels in a 3 × 3 kernel. The
smoothing despeckle filter replaces the center pixel of a 3 × 3 kernel with the median value of the
kernel. This is the default setting for acquisitions that are not a movie exposure.
To change between the two filters, in the [Imaging] section of the sri.ini file set the
parameter that follows:
DespeckleAlgorithm=0 Smoothing despeckle filter
DespeckleAlgorithm=1 Salt and pepper noise filter
4.3.8 Description of the image capture procedure
When the trigger system starts an image capture, the imaging system software uses the energy,
dose rate or information received from the DCB to select and load the applicable correction
images. An HT on signal from the DCB CAN bus causes the imaging system software to capture
image frames and shows them as 32 × 32-bit thumbnail images. When the thumbnail images
become more than a pixel threshold value that is set in the sri.ini file, the imaging system
software starts to count the image frames.
It is necessary for the frame averaging to have a specified number of frames to make an image.
Make a selection from:
• Off (does not average frames).
• Low (FrameAvgNormal)
• Medium (FrameAvgMedium)
• High (FrameAvgHigh)
• Maximum (captures frames for the complete beam).
The parameters in brackets are set in the sri.ini file for each image type.
The imaging system software stops the image capture after it collects the specified number of
frames and HT is on when it captures the last frame. If the HT goes off before the last frame is
completed, the imaging system software continues to capture the specified number of images.

4.3.9 Description of the detector panel alert
The MV detector panel Alert Level messages tell the user when damage can occur to the MV
detector panel by too much radiation.
When the imaging system software receives an HT on signal from the DCB, it does an analysis of
the thumbnail images for radiation in the frame. If the analysis finds a pixel output value above a
specified threshold, there is radiation in the frame.
The imaging system software then does an analysis of each pixel in the thumbnail to find the
brightest pixel. This is defined as x. The analysis continues to find the brightest pixel at the edge of
the four sides of the thumbnail. This is defined as y. If y is greater than the Alert Level threshold
value, the Alert Level 3 message is displayed. If the ratio (y/x) is greater than the Relative
threshold value, the Relative Alert Level 3 message is displayed. The analysis continues for
Alert Level 2 then Alert Level 1.
The Alert Level and Relative threshold values are different for the AL panel (non-applicable for
Harmony) and the AP panel.
An Alert Episode starts when the analysis finds an Alert Level and continues for the time of the
radiation beam. If the user cancels the Alert Level message, no more messages are displayed
unless there is a change in the Alert Level.
4.3.10 Description of the detector panel lifetime image
The lifetime image is the collected images that make up all the exposure on the MV detector
panel in Clinical and Service Mode. The collected dose images are saved as images of 32 × 32-bit
pixels.
It is possible to export the lifetime image to a folder as a .HIS or a .CSV file from Service > AmSiSpecific Service Functions > Export Panel Lifetime Image (Clinical or Service). To see the .HIS file,
use the XIS software. To see the .CSV file, use a worksheet program such as Microsoft® Excel.
The MV detector panel statistics for the lifetime image are available from Service > AmSi-Specific
Service Functions > View Panel Usage Statistics. The statistics give the information that follows:
• Total frames acquired
• Total frames acquired with radiation on
• Total frames acquired that were corrected
• Total frames that have more than a specified brightness
• Total number of Alert Level messages.

4.3.12 Description of the event log files
There are five log levels (0 to 4) configured in the sri.ini file to set the type of messages that
the event logs collect.
• LogLevel 0 (or no log entry) records no messages
• LogLevel 1 are information messages (all messages)
• LogLevel 2 are minor messages (includes LogLevel 3 and LogLevel 4
messages)
• LogLevel 3 are important messages (includes LogLevel 4 messages)
• LogLevel 4 are messages about errors only
For example, LogLevel 1 records all possible messages. LogLevel 3 records the the error and
important messages only.
The iCom-Vx event log includes the information that follows:
• Date and time the iCom-Vx mode starts
• Current information about the patient, the treatment and the fields selected. This
includes the date and time
• New patient information, which includes the treatment and the fields selected. This
includes the date and time
• Date and time iCom-Vx mode ends
• Date and time of an unusual disconnect.
It is possible to change the operation of the iCom-Vx event log. In the sri.ini file below
[Icom], set LogAppend=1 to add a new event log to a current event log. Set LogAppend=0 to
make a new event log each time you start the imaging system software.
By default, the event log file for the imaging system software event log is in D:\iview\logs
\sri.log and the the event log file for iCom-Vx is in D:\iview\logs\icom.log.

4.3.15 Description of IMRT dosimetric weighting
The dosimetric weighting parameter determines how the imaging system software weights the
individual segment images when performing a Multi-Exposure (that is, "2/n") acquisition with an
IMRT beam delivery (Refer to iViewGT™ Instructions for Use).
The default operation after normalization is to equally weight each of the segment images for the
composite image result. Use dosimetric weighting if there are different segment doses and it is
necessary that each of the segment shapes are in view in the image. When imaging for dosimetry
with external third party EPID Dosimetry equipment, it is possible that the weight of individual
images is set to the collected pixel values of each segment.
To enable dosimetric weighting in the sri.ini file, find the [Imaging] section and set
parameter IMRTDosimetricWeighting to 1. To enable the default operation of equal
weighting, set IMRTDosimetricWeighting to 0 or remove the parameter completely.
If there is a license for EPID Dosimetry, the imaging system ignores the
IMRTDosimetricWeighting parameter and applies dosimetric weighting to all images.
4.3.16 Description of the CAN bus monitor system
The imaging system software continuously monitors the CAN bus messages from the DCB. The
monitor system prevents irradiation of the patient if you cannot get an image of the patient
position.
If a message does not appear for 10 seconds, there is no communication with the DCB. The
Communication lost with the DCB. message is displayed on the screen.
The user must acknowledge the message to clear it. If the imaging system software does not
receive CAN bus message from the DCB after 10 seconds, the message will appear again.

The angular movement stops before the pins engage. The arm looks open, but it is not locked in
position by the pins. The fully open condition is when the detector lock solenoid is de-energized
to let the longitudinal movement operate. When the solenoid de-energizes, there is a sound as
the latch disengages from the slot in the detector arm.
The microswitches are continuously monitored during the movement. The closed microswitch
senses if the arm is in the closed position. Microswitches Open A and Open B sense when the pins
engage on each side of the detector. A valid open command overrides these microswitches (it is
valid for the detector arm to be not fully open or fully closed during movement).
If the movement pauses between the open and closed positions, the host touchguard chain
breaks and the buzzer sounds. To start movement again, press the OPEN or CLOSE buttons and
the ENABLE bars on the HHC.
A power amplifier operates the actuator that rotates the shoulder assembly. The output voltage
of the amplifier goes up linearly to a maximum voltage in approximately one second. When the
command for the movement stops, the output falls to 0 V and one second later the output goes
to a tristate condition. This controls the speed of the motor as it decreases.
When the angular movement completes, the detector lock solenoid de-energizes and the latch
disengages from the slot in the detector arm. If the detector locked microswitch senses that the
solenoid is engaged, the ACB disables the longitudinal movement.
Continuous operation of the OPEN button and the ENABLE bars cause the longitudinal and the
lateral movements to move the MV detector panel to the isocenter position. The longitudinal and
lateral potentiometers are used to sense when the detector panel gets to the isocenter position.
If the contacts of the middle arm retracted microswitch are not in the closed position when the
pivot movement completes, the detector arm logic is incorrect. To correct the logic, the middle
arm moves in the G-direction until the microswitch closes, and then moves the detector arm in
the T-direction. It is possible that the user will see, but does not understand, this very small
movement. The movement enables the correct logic for the middle arm movements, and the
mechanical longitudinal scale to read correctly.
4.5.2 Operation of the close movement of the detector arm (nonapplicable for Harmony)
To close the detector arm, on the HHC press the CLOSE button and the ENABLE bars at the same
time. The detector cradle moves in the A-B direction to move the detector panel to the center
position. As the detector panel moves near to the center position, it moves more slowly. The
detector centered microswitch operates when the detector panel is in the center position. The
middle arm then moves in the G-direction until it is fully retracted and the middle arm retracted
microswitch operates.
The detector panel cradle then moves in the G-direction. The detector locking microswitch
operates when the cradle is near to the locked position. This releases the lock solenoid. The
cradle continues to move in the G-direction until it is above the lock solenoid. The lock solenoid
pin latches in to the cradle and operates the detector locked microswitch to stop the movement.
At this time, the middle arm is retracted fully.
If the cradle is retracted fully, it is necessary to move the cradle in the T-direction to close it. This
disconnects the detector locked microswitch, changes the direction of drive gear movement to
the opposite direction. The cradle then moves in the G-direction until the middle arm is fully
retracted and the middle arm retracted microswitch operates.
The close operation does a check to make sure that the conditions that follow are correct.
• The detector panel is in the center position
• The detector cradle is locked.

Description of the movement system of the detector arm
Note: On later versions of the iViewGT™ MV detector arm, the Open B microswitch is not installed and
only the Open A microswitch conditions apply.
If the conditions are correct, the detector arm starts to rotate to the vertical position. Before this
occurs, the ACB retracts the the A-side and B-side lock pins and the Open A and Open B
microswitches are disconnected. The interlock through the Open A microswitch removes the
power from the lock solenoid. This prevents incorrect movement of the cradle. The interlock
opens and there is an audible alarm if:
• The status of the detector centered microswitch is incorrect
• The status of the detector locking microswitch is incorrect
• The movement stops.
The detector arm continues to rotate to the vertical position until the pivot closed microswitch
operates.
4.5.3 Center movement of the detector panel (Harmony only)
The center movement moves the detector panel from any position to the isocenter position.
Operation of the CENTER PANEL button and the ENABLE bars cause the longitudinal and the
lateral movements to move the MV detector panel to the isocenter position. The longitudinal and
lateral potentiometers are used to sense when the detector panel gets to the isocenter position.
4.5.4 Description of the longitudinal movement of the detector arm
The longitudinal movement (G-T direction) has two separate movements:
• The detector panel moves in relation to the middle arm
• The middle arm moves in relation to the shoulder casting.
These movements are referred to as the detector drive and middle arm drive.
One drive motor controls the two movements. A clutch and a brake transfer the drive motor
movement in one direction or the other.
When the detector arm moves from the retracted position (G-direction of the longitudinal
movement), initially the detector cradle moves in relation to the middle arm. The detector cradle
moves to the detector imaging position (to minimize the backscatter into the detector). The
detector imaging position microswitch operates and the movement changes to the middle arm
drive. The middle arm drive then moves the detector cradle to the applicable position in the G-T
direction.
When the detector arm retracts, the middle arm moves in the G-direction until the middle arm
retracted microswitch operates. The movement then changes to the detector cradle drive. The
detector panel cradle then moves in the G-direction. For Harmony, the cradle will move in the G-T
direction until the arm is retracted fully. For non-Harmony, the detector locking microswitch
operates when the cradle is near the locked position. This releases the lock solenoid. The cradle
continues to move in the G-direction until it is above the lock solenoid. The lock solenoid pin
latches in to the cradle and operates the detector locked microswitch to stop the movement. At
this time, the arm is retracted fully.
If you press the IMAGING ASU button together with the ENABLE bars on the FKP, automatic
remote retraction of the detector panel occurs.

Description of the movement system of the detector arm
4.5.4.1 Illegal logic status
If the control logic of the longitudinal movement reaches a status where the control system does
not know the longitudinal position, the manual brake release buttons flash and the longitudinal
movement is disabled. This continues until the logic is corrected.
This condition occurs when:
• The detector cradle is NOT at the imaging position (so backscatter may be introduced
into the image), AND
• The middle arm is NOT fully retracted (so, for non-Harmony, the longitudinal scale is
incorrect; for Harmony, the covers are not aligned).
If the manual brake release is operated, the detector cradle can be manually moved to a correct
logic status, that is, a known position. By de-selecting the manual brake release, the arm can be
driven normally.
4.5.4.2 Isocenter pause
When approaching the imaging position, longitudinal movement is slowed down at
approximately 2 cm (depending on calibration) before the imaging position is reached. This is
independent of direction (not as visible as in the lateral movement), and permits a more accurate
pause. When the imaging position is reached, the movement is paused for approximately 1
second to allow the user to stop at the imaging position.
The longitudinal coarse potentiometer is used to determine the position at which to reduce the
movement speed. The potentiometer voltage is compared with a known voltage, which is set
during calibration.
Using a similar voltage comparator system, the fine potentiometer is used to detect when the
panel is at the imaging position. Movement is paused for approximately 1 second.

4.5.4.3 Longitudinal extended limit
When the longitudinal movement reaches the furthest position from the gantry, the longitudinal
coarse potentiometer is used to detect the limit using a voltage comparator. When the limit has
been reached, only movement away from the limit is possible, that is, towards the gantry.

The lateral movement is driven using a leadscrew system and does not have a manual brake
release.
4.5.5.1 Isocenter pause

approximately 2 cm (depending on calibration) before the imaging position is reached. This is
independent of direction (not as visible as in the lateral movement), and permits a more accurate
pause. When the imaging position is reached, the movement is paused for approximately 1
second to allow the user to stop at the imaging position.
The longitudinal coarse potentiometer is used to determine the position at which to reduce the
movement speed. The potentiometer voltage is compared with a known voltage, which is set

Using a similar voltage comparator system, the fine potentiometer is used to detect when the

4.5.5.2 Description of the lateral movement limits
The lateral coarse potentiometer is used to determine the limits of the lateral movement. When
the lateral movement reaches the limit, the only movement possible is away from the limit.
4.5.6 Description of the touchguard system of the detector arm
The ACB stops the detector arm movements when:
• There is a collision with the touchguard and the touchguard system operates
• The linear accelerator removes the host movement PSU voltage (PSU host healthy).
These effects open the power relays on the ACB for approximately two seconds and stop all
movements on the detector arm. The ACB also breaks the host linear accelerator touchguard
interlock at the same time. The detector arm waits for a response from the host digital
accelerator to confirm the touchguard status.
The detector arm has a detector touchguard and a middle arm touchguard (non-aplicable for
Harmony).

5.2.17 Correcting an unwanted noise that occurs during gantry rotation
It is possible that the sound comes from the counterbalance weight on the iViewGT™ and the XVI
detector arm . The counterbalance weight moves from side to side during gantry rotation and it is
possible that the spring comes into contact with the pin.
1 Rotate the gantry to 90°.
2 Remove the cover to get access to the actuator.
Note: The counterbalance assembly is at the bottom of the actuator.
3 Pull the counterbalance weight near to you, and look at the spring and pin.
It is possible to see if the spring comes into contact with the pin.
4 Apply a thin layer of grease on the pin.
5 Carefully put the counterbalance weight in the correct position.
6 Install the cover.

5.4.2.7 Could not initialize the detector control board monitor
5.4.2.7.1 Correcting an initialization failure of the detector control board monitor
When the iViewGT™ program starts, the detector data link sends an initialization signal to the MV
detector panel. The MV detector panel sends a frame synchronization signal to the detector
control board (DCB) PCB. The DCB then sends a message through the controller area network
(CAN) cable to the iViewGT™ program. If this message is not received, it is possible that there is:
• No electrical supply on the DCB.
• A defective trigger cable or connection between the MV detector panel and the DCB.
• A defective CAN cable or connection between the DCB and the iViewGT™ control
cabinet.
• A defective DCB.
• A defective USB CAN card.
• A problem with the CAN software driver.

synchronization emulated
If you cannot find the cause of the Could not initialise detector control
board monitor error through troubleshooting with the detector control board (DCB) DIP
switch 4 set to ON, you can set the switch to OFF to help troubleshoot the problem. With the DCB
DIP switch 4 set to OFF, the firmware in the DCB emulates the frame synchronizations from the
MV detector panel. The iViewGT™ program does not receive the initial CAN message from the
DCB PCB when the DCB simulates the frame sync. It is possible that are one or more of the
following faults:
• There is no supply voltage on the DCB PCB.
• There is a defective cable between the DCB and USB CAN card in the iViewGT™ control
cabinet.
• The DCB PCB is defective.
• The USB CAN card is defective.

5.4.3.4 Correcting the no image acquired error (AL panel (non-applicable for Harmony))
The Usable frame acquired counter at the bottom left of the screen continuously reads 0. This
includes when radiation is on, after the Waiting for beam to come on dialog box closes.
In most conditions, the cause is a bad connection along the data cable which runs from the MV
detector panel to the iViewGT™ control cabinet (detector, gantry, reeling post assembly or RIC
and iViewGT™ control cabinet).
1 If the message No image acquired. Exposure to image detector can
be too low. appears, examine the connection points along the image data cable.
2 Make sure that the thresholds for Beam on in sri.ini are set correctly.
3 Make sure that the power cable is connected correctly to the power supply and make sure
that no pins are damaged.
4 Examine the LEDs on the power supply.
5 Examine the PSU for the MV detector panel with the cable disconnected from the MV
detector panel. Look at the connector face on.
The pin configuration is from the left, with the notch at the top. 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 are in a
counterclockwise direction.
The voltages at the end of the cable must be:
– Pin 1 to pin 3 = + 12.5 V
– Pin 2 to pin 3 = - 12.5 V
– Pin 5 to pin 4 = 5.5 V.

and iViewGT™ control cabinet).

be too low. appears, examine the connection points along the image data cable.

and UtilBeamOnThreshold in the sri.ini are set correctly.

It is possible that you can see some synchronization lines in the gain calibration and clinical

synchronization fault and the distance between the stripes is the same.

correction.

5.10 Bad pixel map
The manufacturer of the MV detector panel makes the bad pixel map during the assembly of the
panel. A CD with a copy of the bad pixel map is supplied with each MV detector panel.
iViewGT™ calculates new values for the pixels in the bad pixel map. The new value is calculated
from the values of pixels that are in the same area as the bad pixel.
There are three types of bad pixel:
• Black pixels
• White pixels (can also be seen as a white line)
• Noisy pixels
This section shows how to use the XIS software to add more bad pixels to the current bad pixel
map.
There are four procedures:
1 6σ (sigma)
2 Black and White
3 Flood Image
4 Phantom Image.
The 6σ (sigma) and Black and White procedures identify the pixels with values that deviate by a
large amount from the average pixel value (these are black and white pixels).
The Flood Image and Phantom Image procedures identify and remove noisy pixels or individual
bad pixels (these show up against white or gray backgrounds).
Bad pixel map procedures are supplied for both MCLi™, MCLi2™, Beam Modulator™ and Agility™
BLDs.

5.12 Description of the changes to the MV CAN settings
With the introduction of the detector readback safety kit (DRSK), the Synergy MV CAN bus has an
increased bus length. Because of this increased bus length, the CAN settings were optimized by
introducing two lines into the sri.ini [CAN] section:
SoftingTimeSegment1=13
SoftingTimeSegment2=2
However, the values for the SoftingTimeSegment parameter in the DCB utility on current
iViewGT™ releases are hard-coded and are different to the values above. This could cause
incorrect fault messages when fault-finding the MV CAN bus after a DRSK installation (see Figure
5.56). To prevent this problem, go back to the pre-DRSK MV CAN configuration (see Figure 5.57),
before fault-finding the MV CAN bus.

6.1 Important information for the repair and replacement of
service parts
This chapter contains the procedures for the removal, installation, and replacement of iViewGT™
service parts. For more information about the available iViewGT™ service parts, see the Digital
Accelerator Service Parts Manual.
WARNING 6.1
Do not operate the imaging system after you replace or disconnect parts until you do a check of
the operation of the touchguards and stop motors. The touchguards and stop motors must
operate correctly. If you ignore this warning, you can cause serious injury and damage to the
equipment.
WARNING 6.2
Do not install screws that have a red paint mark without the use of Loctite®. If you remove or
replace screws that have a red paint mark, you must apply Loctite® to the thread before you
install them and apply red paint as a witness mark. If you ignore this warning, you can cause
fatal injury, clinical mistreatment and damage to the equipment.
WARNING 6.3
Do not work on the detector arm until you make sure that you cannot move the detector panel
from the control room. If you ignore this warning, you can cause serious injury.
WARNING 6.4
Do not put hands or fingers in the path of the parts of the detector arm that move. When you
use manual movements, pull or push the detector arm from the front of the detector panel
only. If you ignore this warning, you can cause injury and damage to the equipment.
Note: Do the procedures in this chapter with the gantry at 0° and the MV detector arm is at isocenter,
unless the procedure tells you differently.

6.11 iViewGT™ control cabinet
6.11.1 Description of the data backup procedures
The backup procedures make a backup of the data on each of the hard disk drives in the
iViewGT™ control cabinet. The drive C backup saves the operating system configuration and
calibrations made to the iViewGT™ control cabinet. The drive D backup saves the patient
database and related data files information. You can use the backups to restore the operating
system and patient database if you have to replace a hard disk drive or a fault occurs.
You must make a drive C backup after the initial calibration is completed. It will not then be
necessary to do a full system calibration, which decreases the system downtime.
You must make a backup of the iViewGT™ patient database and related data files daily. You can do
the backup with the Windows Backup Utility.
It is necessary to use the Snapshot, backup and restore CD to do the backups. You can save the
backup files to a DVD or to a network location.

6.13.5.3.1 Configuring the energy signatures

energy signatures.

6.13.7 Multilevel gain calibration
Use this procedure to reduce image artifacts that include watermarks.
The function of the multilevel gain procedure is to acquire a series of images each with a different
radiation dose level. Use one or more of these procedures to reduce the radiation dose level
when you acquire the images.
1 Irradiate with a lower PRF. This is the easiest procedure, but the DCB parameters are not
stable at a PRF less than 4. This can have an effect on an imaging system with the AL
detector panel (not applicable for Harmony) more than an imaging system with the AP
detector panel.
2 Adjust the Low Power phase control (LP.ph.crtl) at a PRF less than 4.
3 Use the XVI water tank if available or acrylic sheets to get the necessary attenuation. Elekta
recommends that you use acrylic sheets of size 300 x 300 x 180 mm.
It is not necessary to do a MLG calibration for all energies. If X-Low is the usual imaging energy,
then only do a MLG calibration for X-Low.
The time to do a full MLG calibration is much longer than the time to do a standard single-level
calibration. Elekta recommends that you only do a MLG calibration if it is necessary.
The MLG calibration procedure has the steps below:
1 Configure the station service settings to do a setup of the sri.ini parameters.
2 Do a setup of the linear accelerator parameters for MLG calibration for PRF 6 or PRF 7.
3 Offset calibration. This is applicable to all BLDs.

images after you do this procedure. This is because of a problem with the correction hardware at
a PRF that is less than 4. There is not a solution for this problem.
You can use this procedure to do a five level or a four level gain calibration if you ignore the
lowest levels.
1 Log on to the imaging system software as a service2 user.
2 In the database area, select the Service radio button, and then click OK.
3 In the Service menu, select Station Service Settings.
The sri.ini opens in Notepad.
4 Browse to the [Calibration] section and set the parameters that follow:
– CalibrationFloodLevelsLow=7
– CalibrationFloodLevelsMedium=1
– CalibrationFloodLevelsHigh=1
Note: These parameters set the number of gain calibration levels.
5 Do the offset calibration.
6 Do the first radiation synchronization calibration.
7 Find and record the dose rate for each calibration level:
– For MLG level 7 use the maximum dose rate of the linear accelerator
– For MLG level 6 select PRF 6 by dividing the maximum dose rate by 2
– For MLG level 5 select PRF 5 by dividing the maximum dose rate by 4
– For MLG level 4 select PRF 4 by dividing the maximum dose rate by 8
– For MLG level 3 select PRF 3 by dividing the maximum dose rate by 16
– For MLG level 2 select PRF 2 by dividing the maximum dose rate by 32
– For MLG level 1 select PRF 1 by dividing the maximum dose rate by 64.
8 Do the gain calibration for all energies. Start at MLG level one with the lowest dose rate (see
Table 6.17).
Note: Set the gun servo to manual for PRF 1, 2 and 3, the gun is not stable at these low PRF settings. Set
the manual current to get the usual full load current.

7.1.1 Description of the amorphous silicon AP detector panel
The detector panel is an Amorphous Silicon (a-Si) sensor array with a Gadox Green scintillator.
The scintillator converts incident X-Ray radiation to visible light, which the sensor array captures.
The peak sensitivity of the sensor array is at the wavelength of green light.
The sensor array has a resolution of 1024 pixels × 1024 pixels set at a pitch of 400 µm. The
detector panel weighs approximately 8.5 kg with dimensions of 500 mm × 560 mm × 22 mm. The
active sensor area is 410 mm × 410 mm.
The detector panel uses 16-bit ADCs for high dynamic range and contrast, and has a read out rate
of 15 frames per second through a Gigabit Ethernet connection. The X-ray interface contains a
built-in trigger system.
The iViewGT™ control system reads the image data from the detector panel through an Ethernet
data connection in the control cabinet.
